questions.q: What is the author's main argument?
options: The religious left is a new political force born in this election
Black Christian women have long been the left's steadiest supporters
White evangelical voters are shifting steadily toward Democrats
Black churches should stop reserving senior leadership for men
questions.explain: The author says the religious left is not new and that Black Christian women have long been the staunchest supporters.

questions.q: What share of Black women voted for Democrats in the 2026 exit polls?
questions.explain: Black women voted Democratic at 93%, compared with 59% of women overall and 86% of Black men.

questions.q: What did Keisha Lance Bottoms say about her decision to run for governor?
options: She prayed on it, and said God told her to go
Her pastor urged her to run after a Sunday service
Her billionaire opponent was a friend of the church
She decided after a Civil Rights anniversary march
questions.explain: She recalled praying about running and said 'God told me to go.'

questions.q: What did Nannie Helen Burroughs say in 1958 that African American Christians wanted?
questions.explain: Burroughs said African American Christians wanted 'Jesus, jobs and justice.'

questions.q: What does the author imply about the post-election coverage of the religious left?
options: It correctly credited Black women for powering the Blue Wave
It overstated how many Muslims and Jews voted Democratic
It treated religious Democrats as new and overlooked Black women
It ignored progressive Christians in favor of white evangelicals
questions.explain: The author says calling religious Democrats a new bauble implies they had been off the ballot, which is not true, especially for Black women.
